utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And before we start, I have to say that in accordance with the Rule 15 bis, Judge Argibay won't be able to join us, and the remaining judge decided to continue the proceedings. Are there any issues that the parties would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber. Yes, Ms. Sinatra. I think lady first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's quite genteel. I just wanted to ask the Court to recognise that Dragan Jokic will not be waiving his right to contest the statements taken by the OTP in 2000 and 1999 because we intend to use Mr. Obrenovic's statement taken at that time to attack his credibility, but not for the truth of the matter asserted within the document. So if the Trial Chamber would recognise it under Article 20, 21, Rules 87, 95, 63 and 42 that we still maintain that not only are Mr. Jokic's interviews illegally taken but also Mr. Obrenovic's interview was probably illegally attained, although we do not have standing to contest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I hear Mr. McCloskey on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have no objection to the use of Mr. Obrenovic's prior statements in his cross-examination, and I don't believe his statement is at issue any longer as evidence in this case, since he was able to testify, and I think the Court's ruling on that matter. So it shouldn't be an issue. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I turn to Mr. Wilson on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My apologies, Your Honour. We have no objection to the statement being used for cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, Ms. Sinatra, your application is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there anything else? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for just a housekeeping matter that will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And for your information --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We are now in open session. And for your information, we cancelled sitting on Friday afternoon, in accordance with Ms. Sinatra's information provided to us yesterday, and I hope we could finish the testimony of this witness as early as possible. And today we'll sit until 7.00, and tomorrow we have the whole day, which means we have to sit until 4.30 tomorrow afternoon. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will certainly try my best to cover the material, and it is probable that we would be finished in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In time. What do you mean by "in time"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: By 4.30 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I said, the earlier the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we could finish this witness Friday morning, during one session or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would like that. I promise I'll be finished by 4.30 on Thursday, but we still need to have court for the redirect and the Judges' questions, I believe, on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Obrenovic, I'm so sorry. I was so hasty in taking the podium yesterday that I forgot to introduce myself. I'm Cynthia Sinatra. I work along with my esteemed lead counsel, Miodrag Stojanovic, and we both represent Dragan Jokic. And I'm sorry I didn't introduce myself yesterday. We had already gone over the outside of the model yesterday and if we could just get one overview of the model from the exterior. I think we're going to go into the model in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Your Honours I'd like to also thank Mr. Frank Swanson who is from the audiovisual department for his assistance in the courtroom today. Thank you. We have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, can you use the pointer again and point to the entrance of the -- I'm just going to call it headquarters, to be brief.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, first of all, thank you for your kind words. The entrance to the building is right here. You can't see very clearly, but it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that entrance faces the highway out front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Facing the road you mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask the usher's assistance now. We're going to go -- the model comes 0, ground floor, first floor and second floor, and if Ms. Usher could please go ahead and take it down to the ground level first, I would appreciate your assistance. Thank you. Now, I don't know if we can get a view from the camera at this time of the ground floor, but, Mr. Obrenovic, could you point with your pointer on the ground floor as to where your entranceway is and where the stairs are. And other than that, there are really no important staff offices on the ground floor, are there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, it appears to me that there is both a statement and a question included in your question. So as for the latter, staff offices, as far as I remember, the ground floor contained the office of the assistant chief of staff for the personnel, administration. I think it was Major Galic at the time. And you came in this way, it was the first office to the left, this one. This is where Major Galic was. He was part of the staff. And then there was the staff office. When I say "staff office," I don't mean the physical office itself, the room. I mean its purpose. There were two persons working there who were part of the staff, and there was the staff office. Not the room itself, but the two people constituting the staff office, as a functional unit, not as a room. I think they were in this room. Then there was the staircase, just opposite --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, excuse me. Is that staff office, that's for administrative recordkeeping for the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can continue going on to the next room.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to point out the staircase for you. It was probably hereabouts. I think this must be the staircase, if I understand the model correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct. Now, the only other office that might be of any other importance on the ground floor would be Mr. Tanacko Tanic's office. Can you point that one out to us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One you've entered through the entrance and then you turn left down the corridor, it's one of these two offices at the far end of the corridor, to the right. This one or this other one. I think this first one was the office for the brigade files and administration. There was a woman working there who was in charge of keeping the files, and if I remember correctly, this last office at the far end of the corridor was the office of the chief of the brigade's finances. And then there was Tanacko whom you've referred to and another man. There were two persons in this office. I think the last one at the far end of the corridor. I may have been mistaken pointing that out, but I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point out the office of the military police also.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was just opposite, across the corridor. You go down this corridor and then at the far end of the corridor, the last office to the left, on the left-hand side of the corridor, I think that was the office of the commander of the military police company and the office just before that one, here, next to the toilet, lavatory, was the office of the crime prevention unit of the military police company. I think those four lawyers were based here in this office, from the military police. That's how I remember it, at least. This has been changed many times over, but that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I'd just like to take a moment, Your Honours. I have forgotten to identify the model as -- I believe it's D9/3, for the record. And it represents the physical exhibit of the model of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. And for purposes of the record, when we finish our discussion of the floors, I will provide Mr. Obrenovic with a copy of the layout so he can mark all the places he's identified to be introduced into evidence, if that's all right with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the way, are you going to tender this model into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how about the resumes and the letters of the model builder?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I don't know whether they've been copied yet. They will be supplied, all the copies will be supplied during the next break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you are going to tender this into the evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to tender into evidence all supporting documents to support the foundation for the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there's no disputes concerning with this model, I don't think, you know, that it's necessary to admit into the evidence the resume of the builders. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would love to not have to introduce it, Your Honour, if the Court finds it sufficient that the witness has identified it and said that it accurately depicts the headquarters in 1995, then we don't need to tender those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, in other case, I think in the Celebici case, a model of the Detention Unit was also tendered as the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Except it took up the whole centre of this courtroom. It was really huge, and it was provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Usher, could we take it now to floor 1, and I hope now that Mr. Swanson can get a view of this. If we can't, we'll put it on the ELMO, but I hope we can get a good view of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a problem, but the witness has -- is I think -- hasn't really been able -- hasn't been asked for the inside yet whether this is his recollection, whether these are accurate. He's, I think, doing his best to point things out, but I don't think that foundational question has been asked. I think it was for the outside, but I don't think we quite got there, and maybe these other floors are more crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is exactly right. We discussed it outside of the courtroom, but he's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, does the layout on the inside of the building fairly accurately depict the way the Zvornik Brigade headquarters looked in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. May I just have another look at the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, you asked me whether the ground floor is faithfully reflected in this model, to the best of my recollection. I can only speak on the basis of my own recollection. The interior of the ground floor of this building is, I think, fairly faithfully reflected, except here, right here, this separation, the wall between these two rooms, I don't think it was there in July 1995. I think there was a hall, a room here, that we used for lining soldiers up. There was a bigger area here. I don't remember this wall being here. There was a widening here, and then the next thing was this wall and the staff office here inside, with the typists and all that. I remember when the Office of the Prosecutor searched the building, we lined ourselves up here, in this room, and that's where it was. This wall, a separation was not in place, and I don't think it was there in July 1995. I may be wrong, but to the best of my recollection it wasn't there. As for the rest of it, I think it faithfully reflects the interior of the building. Obviously I don't know much about the scale to which this model was built, but I suppose that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'd like the record to reflect that the witness has identified one wall that he is questioning. Fortunately, this model has been put together so that walls can be removed and at the next break we will remove that wall to conform with his memory of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. So it's kind of like Legos. Okay, now If you don't mind, can we go to the next floor, which is -- we call it the second floor, in Europe it's referred to as the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, most of the staff, the important officers for the brigade headquarters, were located on this floor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we can get a view of the inside, if it's possible, Mr. Swanson, can you get the inside of the building here? Mr. Obrenovic, will you locate the stairwell, which is where you come up from the ground floor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, it's the same one that I've already pointed out, must be this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then could you start with the first office next to the stairwell. Start with where you think the duty officer location was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like you said, you come out after you've climbed up the staircase, and to the right, the first office on the right-hand side, was the duty -- operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next office next to that was whose office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next office down the corridor was I believe the office of the commander for logistics, Sreten Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next office to that is -- was an operations room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called it the operations room, yes, because there's a difference between the operations centre and the operations room. There was no communication equipment stored here. There were only tables, covered with books, and several maps. That's all that was there. Aside from that, you're right, yes, the operations room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the next office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two offices, the operations department of the brigade. In the first there were administrators, two or three administrators, maybe four, at one time. And the next office was the office of the chief of the operations department, or rather, the operations affairs, Mijo Dragutinovic, Captain First Class by rank. And the next office was my office, chief of staff. The next one after that was the dormitory of the -- or rather, the bedroom of the brigade commander. That's going down the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're just going to deal with this side for a moment. From the duty officer's office to your office, there are basically four offices in between; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could describe that in metres. How many metres would it be from the door of the duty officer to the door of chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably these smaller offices, with the exception of the operations room, were three or four metres across, roughly speaking. The operations room was twice the size of the other rooms. If you -- if we say that the other rooms were three metres across, then the operations room was between 10 and 14 metres across, I believe. This is a very rough estimate. Maybe the description of the building contains the accurate parameters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically, it could be anywhere from 20 to 25 metres between the offices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you identify -- is there a little partition there with the door that separates the chief of staff and the commander from the rest of the building, with a door in it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this model, I would identify the spot as this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. Let's go across the hall. And whose large office was that across the hall from you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only office on the left-hand side, in this section of the corridor, or anteroom, if you like, was the brigade commander's office, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, namely. It's the one I'm pointing out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we have the toilets, and next to the toilets, whose office is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the toilets. And next office was the office of the assistant commander for security, Lieutenant Colonel [sic] Drago Nikolic, this one right here. Now we're walking back down the corridor. Next to his office was the office of the assistant chief of staff for intelligence affairs, Captain First Class Dusko Vukotic and his personal clerk. There was another security clerk together with this assistant there. The next office was the office of the chief of communications, Captain First Class Milisav Petrovic. The next one was the office of Major Dragan Jokic, chief of engineering, if I remember correctly. Because there were changes. We are, of course, talking about July in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This office was the office of the morale section. Nenad Simic was here, the moral guidance section. And there were three other persons in the room with him. And another toilet, two toilets, actually, one functional, the other was out of order. It was closed. And the next room we used to refer to it as kitchenette. That's how the officers referred to it. There were several tables in there that the officers used to assemble and drink coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we go across the hall from the cafeteria. Is that Commander Milenko Jovanovic's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was Milenko Jovanovic's office, but he wasn't the commander. He was what we called komandir. And that was his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position was commander, or komandir, of the staff command. It's a small unit directly subordinate to the chief of staff, and its task was, to make matters as simple as possible, to ensure the basic requisites for life in the command, that is to say, food, water, tents if they were going in the field. And he was in charge of keeping this area clean, making coffee. His staff would make coffee, bring in food, and so on. And his office was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now could we go on to the second floor, if Ms. Usher can help.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add something, please. This partition here, as we called it, there was a double door here and the commander ordered them to be set up so as to make a separate part of this corridor. It was partitioned off. There was a small hall here, not like this one here, not as it's built up here. The left part of the door was always closed. The right-hand side opened towards this door here. And when you went into this anteroom, on the left-hand side you would come across two doors again. So the left door would lead into the toilets and the second door would lead into the commander's office. On the right-hand side was the entrance to my office. That door was first, this one here, nearest the door. And then there was the room that the commander used to sleep in. So in this separate little hallway, we didn't have three offices on the right-hand side, as this model shows. I remember that clearly. There was my office and then there was the room that the commander used as his bedroom. So two on the right, two on the left. And then three doors on the left-hand side. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I don't think so. I think I'm right in remembering it being that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That sounds fairly accurate too. But the partition was put up so that the commander and the chief of staff could have some privacy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This door was placed there because the commander ordered that in 1993, I believe. The courier was here. And the switchboard used to be here at one time, that is to say, a table with the inboard switchboard, which would sometimes be manned by a man, other times by a woman. And the commander instructed this door to be put up, and, of course, for the reason you state, for privacy, quite certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And for clarity purposes. In July of 1995, the switchboard was not on the first floor, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're quite right. It was not. The switchboard was transferred to the duty officer's room, the operations duty officer. Otherwise, it was up at this wall. But all the devices were moved. This might have been at the beginning of April 1995, for instance, thereabouts, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you also: The duty officer's door had a sign on it that it was to remain shut because of the communications; is that correct, closed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably right. The commander did insist that the door be kept closed. Now, whether there was a sign on the door, I really can't remember. But it would be logical for them to be asked that the door be kept shut. It was an ordinary door, just like that door over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we -- are you finished with the first floor and we can go to the second floor? Okay. Thank you. Mr. Obrenovic, there's really only two rooms on this second floor that are of interest to this case. If you could please identify the communications room and the encryption room, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, Ms. Sinatra, I didn't go up on the upper storey very often, and I'm not sure I know where -- what you asked secondly was located. But when you come up the staircase and come up to the first floor, I think that the encryption office was the first one, the encryption room, that it was the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know where the communications room was located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The in-house switchboard, and all the attending equipment, if I remember correctly, was in this last room here on the right. As I say, it was an in-house switchboard, and we would have to distinguish between the communications centre. We had that in a container up on the hill above Zvornik. This was an in-house switchboard and it was equipped with all the necessary devices for relay communications. And as I say, I think it was the last room on the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't know how we'd like to do this, but could Ms. Usher give Mr. Obrenovic a copy of the floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I don't know if the Court would like for him to fill in the rooms at the break or if you'd like for him just to go ahead and mark on the documents to be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe during the break, and after the break you could ask some questions according to this map. And I hope that each room has a number on it so that we know which room is for what functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take care of that in a moment. It's not numbered at the present, but I will take care of it. That's a very good suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, thank you very much, Mr. Swanson. I think that we're not going to use the model at this point. I just wanted to -- and Ms. Usher. Thank you. The headquarters that's represented there, that's located in a little town called Karakaj, and it's about, would you say, three kilometres north of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the engineering department was about 300 metres away from this compound called Standard, at a place called Sapna? Maybe I'm mispronouncing it. Please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. The interpretation I got was the engineering department. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The engineering department was not located on this compound -- company. The engineering company, I'm sorry, was not located on this compound, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. The engineering company wasn't located there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was located about three kilometres north and on the other side of the highway, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- yes, probably. Now, whether it was three kilometres or not -- but yes, you're right. On the road to Bijeljina, and then you would turn off towards Sapna at the crossroads and find it on the right-hand side. That is, it was opposite the Glinica factory. That's where the engineering company was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for clarification purposes: The duty officer's office that you identified faces the back of the Standard compound, toward the Drina River, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It had a window looking out onto the Drina River, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm kind of jumping ahead because of logistics, but, you know, on the 13th and 14th, supposedly there was a large convoy of prisoners that was transported from Bratunac to the Zvornik area. They went north, in front of this building on the road, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They passed along the road we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm just trying to get some locations down. I know that you stated that on the 14th you were at a location called Snagovo. Please forgive my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you pronounced it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Snagovo is really about ten kilometres or ten minutes from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about ten kilometres. Perhaps it would be best to speak about kilometres rather than the time it takes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, because these roads are not as good as some roads might be; right, during these circumstances in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, you could reach Snagovo along the macadamised road surface, the old road passing by the hospital and up to Snagovo, or you could take the asphalt road across Crni Vrh, which was twice as long. We used, for fast access, the macadamised road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to a different subject, but we've heard several days of testimony from Mr. Nikolic and from you about the military front that was happening from July 4th on through July 16th, 17th, and 18th. So I'm not going to revisit that line of questions with you, but I'm going to ask you three or four summary questions to get that over with. I believe that the testimony that you've given on direct was that on the evening of the 13th of July, you were first informed by Drago Nikolic, the chief of security, that it was the intention of the Main Staff to bus detained prisoners captured during the Srebrenica operation north; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a day earlier, on the 12th of July, you were informed that the 28th Division of the BiH army was fleeing the Srebrenica area and moving toward Tuzla, and Zvornik was right in the way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, without going into detail, that would be it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 15th of July, you were under severe attack by the Muslim column, the 28th Division moving up from the south and from the west/north-west, you were being attacked by the 2nd Battalion of the BiH army, and you were in a very severe situation which could have caused the fall and the loss of Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, this serious fighting had already begun on the evening of the 14th. We had seven dead, in fact, on the night of the 14th, seven of our soldiers had already been killed, which is serious. And on the 15th, yes, this culminated, reached a peak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to explain is that simultaneously with the fact that some security and intelligence officer has informed you that you're going to be flooded with 3.000 to 5.000 prisoners, you're also under attack from every front and undermanned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but may I just add something, and that is that he didn't speak about figures, how many prisoners would be brought in. He just spoke about a large number. So at that time, I didn't know whether it would be 5.000 or however. But in all other respects, you're quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you kept getting misinformation about the size of the column approaching, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Up until the evening of the 13th. On the evening of the 13th, they told me that the column was three kilometres long. On the 14th I saw it for my very own eyes in the morning, although even at that time, just to make a remark, they didn't believe me at the time, and they probably told Major Jokic that they're lying, that it wasn't that way. When I say "everyone," I mean the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, also I want to recap your testimony yesterday regarding Mr. Blagojevic's defence. Basically, you confirmed that most of the information and communication that was travelling around on the 13th and 14th was really being communicated through security and intelligence channels versus directly to commanders who most needed the information at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right when it refers to the work of the security organs, but we had a parallel -- or let me put it this way. Drago Nikolic did report through his own chain, as I said yesterday when I was asked by Mr. Karnavas. I explained this. I don't want to go into details again. But there was the regular chain of command as well, the regular line, whether it was me or whether it was somebody else later on, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, or the duty officer. It didn't matter who, but depending on the day, it was a different man every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just want to bring to light also -- I don't think we've discussed up to now the difference between security and intelligence. And I will introduce a chart in a moment to try to explain it. But the difference between the Bratunac Brigade, which Mr. Nikolic was a part of, and the Zvornik Brigade, which you were deputy commander and chief of staff of, was that the Bratunac Brigade was a light infantry brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, as a light infantry brigade, their offices at the military police, security and intelligence, were all incorporated into one person, Mr. Momir Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes. Now, I'm not quite sure whether Momir Nikolic had a clerk or two clerks, or rather, assistants, people helping him. I think he did have an assistant for security, but he did have one for intelligence affairs [as interpreted]. But all this in the light brigade, not only the Bratunac Light Brigade, all these affairs were seen to by the security person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas in contrast, the Zvornik Brigade had a separate chief of intelligence and chief of security and head of the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they were a regular brigade, not a light brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an infantry brigade. It was an infantry brigade. We had the chief for security, who was at the same time assistant to the commander for security, directly subordinate to him, one of his assistants; and then we had another person and a whole sector, the two of them, in fact, the assistant now of the chief of staff. To me and not Pandurevic, for intelligence, at the headquarters. So this is a significant difference with respect to the Bratunac Brigade, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the responsibilities of Momir Nikolic were distributed between Dusko Vukotic and Drago Nikolic, and is his name Jasikovac, the military police? And then the MUP, the civilian police, was headed by -- was it Borovcanin or was it Vasic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. There are so many parts in that, and we do have two Nikolics here, and I know it gets slightly confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I see whether I've strayed in the correct form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Zvornik Brigade, you had Drago Nikolic, who represented the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had Dusko Vukotic, who represented the chief of intelligence, if I'm right. And you had -- I think his name was Jasikovac. That was commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Miomir Jasikovac was commander of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then another branch of a police protection unit was the MUP, the ministry of -- I'm sorry. I forgot. I'm sorry. MUP stands for Ministry of the Interior, and that was headed by -- was it Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I understood your question properly, but you're right, Borovcanin was the chief of staff of the special police in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, the MUP. But this was a separate entity from the Zvornik Brigade. He wasn't actually a member of the Zvornik Brigade himself. He appeared there on the 15th with the commander of the detachment, sometime around noon, if I remember correctly, and he took part in the fighting at Baljkovica. He wasn't organisationally and establishment-wise a member of the Zvornik Brigade. I'm not sure whether I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. The MUP was part of the civilian entity versus the military entity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the MUP also had a special police brigade, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was headed by Commander Saric, underneath Borovcanin? Or who commanded the special police brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the commander of the special police brigade in July 1995 -- I'm not sure of his rank. I think he was colonel. But anyway, Goran Saric. I think he was a colonel at that time and was promoted somewhat later to general. So he was chief of staff, like I was to Pandurevic, was Lieutenant Colonel Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. I want to go on to your statements recently since you pled guilty. You're absolutely positive that you were not at the headquarters on the 14th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely and absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're telling us that between 6.30 and 7.00 on the morning of the 14th, you weren't at the flag raising or the ceremony that all the soldiers have in which you issue their daily orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I absolutely was not present, and even if I wasn't present, I don't think that the ceremony took place at all on the 14th, because there was general chaos, and I don't think anybody would have thought of doing anything like that. I wasn't there. I wasn't at the barracks. But in view of the situation as it was, and we all know what the situation was like, I don't think anybody would have gone through that ceremony on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you're also saying that you weren't present for the 7.00 to 8.00 meeting at the headquarters, with all the commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if someone saw you there, they'd be wrong; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that I wasn't there. Now ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you left the brigade command on the 13th and that you didn't return until the morning of the 15th, at 11.00. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that I left my office and the headquarters on the evening of the 13th, after talking to General Zivanovic, perhaps half an hour later. Now, the people tapping into the conversation, if they identified it as being at 2030 hours, then quite certainly I had left at 2100 hours. And I already reached Jevtic as dusk was falling, or Maric. So that is the 13th. And I returned on the morning of the 15th. I said in my statement that it was difficult to say exactly what the time was when I arrived. But for orientation purposes, I was able to set the time approximately, because as we were moving towards the barracks from the Zvornik road, we found one of the trucks belonging to the Vukovi -- the Wolves coming back, and then the last intercepted conversation of mine, as Lovac 1 - that was the code - that was recorded at 10.45 or 10.40. So those two parameters help me pinpoint the time. And to the best of my recollection, of course, I knew that it was sometime during the morning, the first half of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lovac 1 was your call-signal on the radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Conversation that you had with Mr. Zivanovic, there's no intercept or proof of that conversation, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we're thinking of the same thing, but there is an intercepted conversation at -- registered on the 13th of July, 1995, at 2035 hours, if I remember correctly, in the evening. It says Obrenovic and the general. And I know that that was General Zivanovic, although it doesn't say Zivanovic; it just says the general. Obrenovic and the general. And I'm talking about the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On the night of the 13th, you are aware that there was a very infamous meeting held in Bratunac where the commanders, along with Popovic and Beara, made the decision that they would have to kill the prisoners? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence. No problem with leading questions, but it has to reflect the reality of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, you may put your question in the form of a question. Ask whether this witness knows there's a meeting or not, and who took part in that meeting, step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a very significant meeting held in Bratunac on the evening of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of ever mentioning anything like that. I was not aware of that meeting. I don't know if it was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the commander, Pandurevic, never mentioned about having attended the meeting in Bratunac where the decision was made to kill the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never referred to anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As deputy commander, you were the commander at the Zvornik Brigade when Commander Pandurevic was fighting in the Krivaja 95; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As chief of staff, I was also the deputy, automatically, while the commander was away, for any reason whatsoever, in relation to your question. In Srebrenica, when the commander was there, when the commander was not in Srebrenica, during his absence, as his deputy, I commanded those units of the Zvornik Brigade units that were in Zvornik at the time, because we did have five or six other units in other places at the time, but I had nothing to do with those. I was only in charge of those units that were in Zvornik at the time, the Zvornik Brigade units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 13th to 14th, Sreten Milosevic was the duty officer, operations duty officer, at the headquarters, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On the 13th it was Sreten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 14th to the 15th, the duty officer was Dragan Jokic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 15th to the 16th, the duty officer was Nenad Simic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the 15th it was supposed to be Drago Nikolic, and on the 16th it was supposed to be Nenad Simic, but there were changes there due to the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Simic was there to assume the duty shift from Dragan Jokic on the morning of the 15th, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because on the 15th, I was not there in the morning, nor was I in charge of the shift on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But don't you have to sign, as chief of staff or deputy commander, in a shift book, when there's a change of duty officers, to confirm it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, if the situation is regular or quiet, if the command functions under relatively normal circumstances, in a manner of speaking, then yes, you would be right. However, if the circumstances were exceptional, even if only on account of a meeting or a briefing, let alone if this exceptional circumstance was as a result of fighting or major disturbances, not only in those days, but also earlier, so on account of that situation, what would usually happen in those days was that the duty officers would agree to change and relieve one another whenever they could. The commander would come and give them tasks, and failing that, they would just go on with their duties as usual and inform the duty operations officer of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come to the exact requirements and descriptions of the duty officer at a later time. The normal procedure would be that you would have to confirm whenever the duty officers change; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. I've just explained that there were exceptions, or aberrations from what you said, and rightly so, was usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The normal procedure would be that you would sign a duty shift book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the shifts were for 24 hours at a time normally, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The duty of the operations duty officer would normally last 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was usually changed between 8.00 and 9.00 a.m. to 8.00 or 9.00 a.m. the following day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember precisely, but the shift was like you said, at 8.00 or at half past 8.00, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And normally the -- I guess he's called a deputy duty officer or assistant duty officer, is prepared to take over for the duty officer between 1.00 a.m. and 6.00 a.m. so that the duty officer can get some rest; is that right, or is it 11.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about midnight or just past midnight. Perhaps it would be more correct to say between 1200 hours, midnight, and about half past 5.00 in the morning, give or take a half hour. The duty officer would sleep and the deputy duty officer would be on duty. And again, if the situation was calm, if the situation was quiet enough to allow him to get some sleep. If not, he would just go on duty or get some rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement also you verified that you filed an interim combat report at 11.00 p.m. on the 14th. You verified that yesterday in your testimony, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I said that most probably I filed it between 2300 hours and 2400 hours. The slip of paper that we read out yesterday, the interim report, and I gave it to the communications officer, who then relayed the message via his radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The normal procedure, though, is that a daily combat report is filed between 5.00 and 7.00 in the evening every day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say precisely, but I think we were supposed to forward interim combat reports to the corps command by 1600 hours, by 1600 hours, regarding the situation at 1500 hours, or maybe one hour later. By 1700 hours, with the situation at 1600 hours. So that the duty officer at the corps could take care of that and to make sure it didn't arrive too late at the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You reviewed that interim combat report yesterday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you filed that interim or extraordinary combat report because of the chaos and threat to the Zvornik Brigade, didn't you? It's not normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the name itself says, it's an interim report. According to the usual procedure, the procedure then in force, interim reports were only forwarded or drafted, rather, when absolutely necessary. That's the long and short of it. I deemed it necessary at the time. We had had many of our soldiers killed or wounded. There was a threat to our units, so I drafted an interim combat report and forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the interim combat report talked about the combat operations that were going on on the 14th on the front there at - excuse my pronunciation - Baljkovica and Snagovo, the front around Zvornik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the front in Snagovo. As for the geographical terms, Snagovo was mentioned, and then the road at Planinci and then the 4th, 6th, and 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this report contained items and descriptions that are considered legitimate military communications, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it totally was descriptive of the combat operations and the need for reinforcements at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no mention of any prisoners coming to the area at that time, was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a legitimate military operation that you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns that report, yes, and that fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you ordered your duty officer to transmit this report; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I wrote this down on a slip of paper. I gave it to the communications officer. Due to technical reasons and because of the equipment that we had, he had to relay this to the radio centre via a radio unit and then the duty officer there would read that to the operations duty officer, and then, obviously, since we have the document, now he gave it to Misko Vasic, who typed it up, and then the document would be coded. That's how it went through the stages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "coded," it would be taken upstairs to the encryption room and slipped through a little slot in the door?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there were two possibilities. The operations duty officer, the duty officer, could call the person who was in charge of encrypting the document. He would say: I have a telegram. And he would come and take it away and maybe the duty officer took the document upstairs himself and brought it to the encryption officer. Now, this depends on the person who was on duty, what exactly was done. Maybe he could have informed the assistant: "Now, take this and take it to the person who was coding the documents." But this is only an assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're stating that you called -- you gave the interim report to your signalman, who called it into the signalman at the headquarters, who then typed it up and gave it to Mr. Jokic? Because there's no intercept information on this interim combat report, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow, I'll repeat this. I wrote it down on a slip of paper, I gave it to my communications officer, the communications officer radioed this to the radio centre, because we couldn't talk to the duty officer directly. You saw that. Zvornik, the headquarters, was in a valley, and it was not physically possible on account of the equipment we had at our disposal. So the person working the radio centre took note of that, phoned the duty officer, read the message out to him. This was a procedure that we had to follow. Now, with Jokic, or the duty officer, would have been supposed to give this to someone to be typed up. We did see yesterday that Misko Vasic was the person who typed it up. And then the next step was for this to be encrypted. Now, your question, why wasn't there an intercepted message? There were a lot of intercepted messages there, but I gave it to the communications officer because he could read it and then put himself in touch with someone else, send it down a different channel, and then there would be someone else there talking on that channel. They would relay one sentence: They're going to Sava 96, and then the next sentence. And this happens not to be there. I wish it was there. I wish we did have it, but we don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So your answer to my question is there is no intercept showing the communication from your signalman at Snagovo to the communications centre about the headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the contents of this interim combat report that we're talking about, yes. But except for that, the registered communication between my communications officer and the radio centre, yes, there are several such things in those days, but not for this specific report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the evidence that we have before us is consistent with you just dictating the interim combat report to Mr. Jokic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. What exactly are you basing your statement on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's another possibility that you weren't at Snagovo and that you directly dictated your interim combat report to Mr. Jokic, and then it was typed by Mr. Vasic and then it was taken to encryption. The only difference is your location when dictating the interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can speculate whatever you like, but I am telling you where I was. And the next thing: On the evening of the 14th, we were crushed in the military sense. We were defeated in that battle. The column of the 28th Division crushed us and threw us to the left, to the west, geographically speaking. And the column was passing between my group and Zvornik. I would not have been physically able to reach Zvornik even if I had wanted to, because our enemy was passing there. Seven of our soldiers were killed. And the next day, in order to reach Zvornik, we had to fight. We had to cut across their path. You have recorded conversations dated the 15th with me saying there are about 300 metres left for us to search and then we'll take the old route, the old road. So on the 15th, days after the event, for the whole night and the next day for several hours we were doing this, so how could we have done anything during the night?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you kind of lost me there with all of that description. But I think what our bone of contention --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just not a military person, so it's very difficult for me to picture in my mind all of these activities. But basically, would you be surprised if Milan Maric had said that you were not at Snagovo on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what to say. I'm telling you: I was at Snagovo on the 14th. Milan Maric, first I hear of him. I don't even know who the person is, or at least it doesn't occur to me at the moment. Yesterday we heard -- or rather, five days ago Mr. McCloskey asked me about a man named Gavric from Bratunac. Yesterday, Mr. Karnavas claimed, he himself claimed that Gavric was not in Zvornik, and yet Gavric said to you that he had seen me there. Therefore, I'm not putting it to you that this Vasic or whatever his name was had not told you something, anything. But what I'm telling you is that I was engaged in combat at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break. Maybe during the break we could read the transcript, Mr. Obrenovic's testimony, to see where we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Have I confused you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I'm quite clear. I'm just afraid that you claim that you did not understand what the witness is telling you. Maybe during the break you could read the transcript for this paragraph, then reorganise your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But what he was describing really is not relevant to my line of questioning. But as far as the military operations, my line of questioning goes -- it can go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we start, Mr. Karnavas, you have something to address the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a brief matter. Mr. McCloskey earlier had objected with respect to a question that was posed by Ms. Sinatra. In fact, there were two questions dealing with a meeting of commanders on the 13th to kill. I didn't -- first, I want to say that I totally agree with the objections and the basis for the objection by the Prosecution. Secondly, I didn't object, one, because I believed Mr. McCloskey had covered it, but in -- after thinking about it, I didn't want the record to reflect that somehow I was acquiescing by not objecting, that somehow there was a meeting of commanders on the 13th, because that was that one question. And then there was a follow-up question about Pandurevic attending a meeting. The facts that we have so far are that there was a meeting on the 13th that we know of, based on the information provided by the OTP between Mr. Deronjic and Beara, Colonel Beara, that Momir Nikolic may or may not have attended, but that's the only meeting. But as far as a meeting of commanders sitting there on the night of the 13th discussing killings, there has been no evidence so far, none has been proposed by the Prosecution, and so I just want to make sure that I do object formally on the record. And my failure to object earlier was out of courtesy to my colleague, but I was not acquiescing to the form of the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand your statement, and it's registered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have one brief housekeeping matter. Yesterday I introduced the original mechanical drawings and architectural drawings from the Standard factory, and if the Court would allow us to substitute copies of these architectural and mechanical drawings, because I promised to return those originals to Standard factory in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I would also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get copies of anything, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it will be furnished to your side when we are going to use it; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution was provided with a courtesy copy several weeks ago. They made the copies in their office for us, and I much appreciate it, but it's the same mechanical drawings that you already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't know what it is, Your Honour. I believe counsel, of course, but if we could just get some idea, then we're fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'd be happy to try to coordinate that information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, I just wanted to go back to the 15th. I know that you claim that you were at Snagovo until the morning of the 15th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you had stated in your direct testimony that you arrived in front of the brigade headquarters about the same time as Dragomir Vasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I entered the compound, the barracks, a moment before Vasic. And then I saw him arrive in a car down the road, through the net, and I waited for him by the kiosk. So we met outside the building, on the road, where the kiosk is, the small kiosk, outside the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had already gone to the barracks before you met Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks, the compound, the gate to the barracks, not the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you went through a whole dialogue of meeting with Mr. Jokic on the morning of the 15th during your direct testimony. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know you're aware that Colonel Dragomir Vasic was the chief of security in the Zvornik area, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dragomir Vasic was the chief of the security centre in Zvornik, of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. The MUP, the civilian branch.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are aware that Colonel Vasic has made several statements to the Prosecutor during the last couple of years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My lawyers received the statements forwarded by the Prosecution, but personally, I don't have any of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you stating before this Trial Chamber today that you don't read any of the witness statements provided to your Defence by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is that I read those of Vasic's statements that the Office of the Prosecutor had forwarded to my lawyers, and therefore to me also. That's the only thing I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to provide for your perusal right now a copy of what has been marked for identification purposes as D16/3. And I'd like to provide it to Madam Usher, over here, Dragoslav Djukic has that and we'd like to provide the witness a copy in B/C/S. Do you have a copy, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I get you to turn to page 48. That's in the English version of Mr. Vasic's statement. It's page 31 in the B/C/S statement, I believe. Mr. Obrenovic, you are aware that this statement by Mr. Vasic was only made on the 10th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the heading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to line 24 of Mr. Vasic's statement, on page 48. I'm not sure what line it is in the B/C/S version. But it says -- it's the paragraph that says: "I read his statement where he said he talked to Jokic, and to be honest, I did not see Jokic. I talked about it several times before, but if I saw Jokic, I would have to say that." Do you see that part? I'm sorry. They're telling me it's page 47, line 17 in the B/C/S version. That's what Mr. Vasic says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he states that Mr. Jokic was not present that morning; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of what it says. He says he didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: All right. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 47 on the English version, line 15. It states that you met Vasic at the headquarters between 9.00 and 10.00, doesn't it? "I called the brigade to see whether Obrenovic was there, because I wanted to see with him, since I've heard that he led those forces above Kula, I wanted to see what happened. And then between 9.00 and 9.30, 10.00 at the most, I went to the brigade." So he's stating that you were at the brigade at 9.00 to 10.00, not 11.00, as you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can read here, it says 9.00, 9.30, 10.00 at the latest, the most. I said before the break that it's very difficult to speak about a precise time after so much time has gone by. But I pinpointed that time on the basis of two facts. First of all, my memory, my recollections of it; and second, that as we were going down the Drina road, we drove up and encountered some trucks that were coming from the Zepa area, the Wolves. And the third thing that helped me pinpoint the time that was there was this intercepted conversation between myself, my code-name was Lovac 1, on that date about 15 to 11.00, at a quarter to 11.00. So it was impossible for somebody to register my conversation -- or register me being in the field at a quarter to 11.00 and to have been in my office at the same time. So I said what I said to Mr. McCloskey and I stand by that. Perhaps Vasic is wrong with the time. Perhaps within an hour or half an hour. So I said approximately around 11.00, give or take 15 minutes. But if they recorded us at 10.45, I couldn't have been in the office, and that's how I arrived at that time. I got to that time. Now, if you expect me to remember the exact time within 15 minutes after so much time has gone by, I really can't do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what you're saying is that you don't really remember what time it was but you've only come up with that time due to refreshing your memory by all of the OTP documents that you've received over the last few years; is that right, including the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I came up with that time on the basis of three factors. First of all, I remember it being during the first half of the day, if it was the morning, I would say it was in the morning. I know that we were fighting that morning and found those dead people up there, the medical corps. And I was also assisted by the documents, what I read in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go on to page 51, line 18, which is, in the B/C/S version -- page 51, line 18. Okay. He'll have to help me. Let me read it for you. Mr. McCloskey says: "What do you think Obrenovic was lying about in the statement that you've read, if anything?" And Mr. Vasic answers: "I think two things: The time of his arrival, the moment that Pandurevic walked in, that he actually talked to us, that the two of us had an argument. And if Obrenovic can remember that he should talk about it. And at the moment that someone said call the air force, I mean, that's really ..." I think that -- isn't Mr. Vasic stating that you mischaracterised or gave false information about several items that he takes -- he contests?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, I think that this is the consequence of the following: That Vasic didn't know the exact time, he couldn't remember whether it was 10.00 or 11.00, for example. That's the first point. And the second point is this: He -- as far as I can it, he read my statement about guilt, which was disclosed, and probably did not have the chance of reading the entire interview. I gave Mr. McCloskey -- actually, my statement as to guilt was an excerpt, a summary. It wasn't the entire interview with Mr. McCloskey. And I explained to Mr. McCloskey the argument and Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic's reactions to Vasic's proposal to let the column pass, and all the rest of it. Now, as to the air force, that he can't remember that, I don't know. I do seem to remember it, and I've already explained why. I thought it was quite amazing. So I couldn't believe that. Now, why he can't remember, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's quite amazing because the VRS didn't have an air force at that point and there was a no-fly zone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska did have an air force. It had an air force brigade, in actual fact, and a helicopter brigade too. But it did not fly because of the NATO no-fly zone, yes, and that's why I was amazed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to your testimony just a second ago. I believe what you just said was that Mr. Vasic's statement, after you pled guilty, that the OTP had provided him with a copy of your plea papers at that time, before he gave his interview. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, Ms. Sinatra. As the plea papers or statement of guilt was on the Internet. Now, I didn't have a chance to speak to Vasic, and you know that full well. I'm just trying to be logical. Vasic is an intelligent man himself, probably looked at the Internet, read my statement of guilt on the Net, and in that statement, there wasn't all this whole section about the meeting where him, Borovcanin, Pandurevic, where they were present, and he was probably adversely affected by that. But as you could have read yourself, I gave detailed explanations about the argument that he mentions here. It wasn't an argument. It was just a different views. Pandurevic said that he was in command, and anybody who wanted to listen could listen, and so on. And I think that Mr. Vasic is referring to that when he mentions this argument here. But that's just a guess on my part again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Vasic's statement before you, I would like to go forward to page 64, line 14, where Mr. Vasic states, mid-paragraph: "I think that Momir Nikolic lied, that he was not with me at the meeting. Some things that Obrenovic mentioned were not correct. And because of the load that I was carrying for a long time, I decided to tell you the things that I kept for myself. My lawyer has already said that there were some nasty messages sent to me from that team." You are aware that Mr. Vasic has made those allegations against you, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what that team means or what this is about or what its relevance is to anything, and just also for the record, the -- since the OTP has been brought up in this, we have not provided Mr. Vasic with a full statement of Mr. Obrenovic, nor is it our policy to do that to suspects that are being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I also got a question in this respect. You said that he was not with me at that meeting. What meeting is it? Maybe you could ask some questions to clarify this point, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Was that on the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this is on the line 15, page 64, you just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I guess I would have to go back. I'm not sure what it refers to in the statement. But basically, all I'm trying to bring out is that Mr. Vasic says that -- and maintains that there have been falsifications in presentation of testimony for the OTP. And I would have to review -- and I could give the Court an answer at the next break on what meeting that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe this is a two-part answer by Mr. Vasic.
