First he's saying Momir Nikolic is not correct about the meeting at the -- I think he's referring to the SDS meeting with Deronjic in Bratunac on the evening of the 13th, and then he goes on to make these other comments about Mr. Obrenovic. So I think that's the context of the answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Your Honours, I'd like to ask to present Mr. Obrenovic with a copy of what has been marked as -- it's Mr. Obrenovic's June 2003 debriefing, and I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but there is a comment here about where Vasic says receiving nasty messages from a team. And Ms. Sinatra has made an accusation against someone, I'm not exactly sure. But if that can be withdrawn from the record. I don't see what she is talking about. And those kind of allegations really are potentially damaging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe Ms. Sinatra promised us that she will look into this matter during the break. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we were referring to that meeting, but that meeting has been clarified by Mr. McCloskey. I was just reading the testimony of Mr. Vasic, and if Mr. Vasic refers to that team, I'm not making any allegations; I'm just stating what the witness stated. And if Mr. McCloskey has any problem with that, then I suppose he can, you know, discredit his own witness. But his own witness, the OTP witness, has stated that. It didn't come from my mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic is a suspect and is certainly not an OTP witness, just to clarify that record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But anyway, Ms. Sinatra, just according to what is said by Mr. Vasic in this statement, I don't see there's any problem. Even if the team refers to the Prosecution's team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe she was referring to someone else, Your Honour, but if she is dropping it, I'll drop it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally have not made any allegations. I was just reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I would not like it to be interpreted that I'm personally making any allegations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be worth reading the record on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But anyway, Ms. Sinatra stated her view very clear just now. I think we have to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: For identification purposes, this is marked as D27/3. Thank you. And this -- please provide Mr. Obrenovic with a copy in B/C/S. Thank you very much. This was the statement of Mr. Obrenovic on the 4th of June, 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 31, of course you stated that you didn't know what time it was that you got back to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, that you based that decision upon the monitored conversations, the tactical ones. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me where that portion is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's line 14, page 31 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And just to save time, Your Honour, the next document will be his April 2nd, 2000 interview from the OTP. And I believe that that's already been marked as a D1 exhibit. I'm not positive. But it is marked as -- do we have it marked? Okay. We don't have it marked. I guess that would be D28/3. And if we could go ahead and provide the B/C/S -- you don't have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I haven't found the previous one either. On page 31, line 14, is empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't have the B/C/S corresponding page number, and I will -- after the next break, I'll come back to this. In fact, since we don't have -- you don't have a copy of your 2nd April, 2000 statement in front of you, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have is what you have given me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then I will go on to the next exhibit, which is marked D19/3, and could we provide the B/C/S copy of that and copies for the usher. This document is the OTP interview of Nenad Simic on 19 September 2001. Mr. Obrenovic, can you just refresh our memory on what Mr. Simic's position was in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, I think he had the rank of captain first class and he was occupying the position of assistant commander for moral guidance, religious affairs, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's the one that went out and met the families after soldiers were killed on the front and took care of funerals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this department's affairs did include assistance at funerals, family members, and so on. I was doing my own job, but it was logical that he probably did attend those funerals, yes, before and after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, Nenad Simic was the person who was to take over the position of operational duty officer on the 15th from Mr. Jokic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was supposed to take over this duty on the 16th. Perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 13 of his statement, line 14. Mr. McCloskey -- I'm sorry. It's Dean Manning. He says: Did you see him or talk to him when he came in on the 15th? And the questioning is whether they saw or talked to Mr. Obrenovic. Then if you go on to page 14, line 6, Mr. Simic says: "I wouldn't know about that, because I met Obrenovic down on the ground floor, and I briefed him quickly about the situation that I was having at the time. I don't know whether they met and talked." And he's talking about whether you met and talked with Commander Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, the form of the question. It was two part, and I believe the first part had to do with Vinko Pandurevic, not Mr. Obrenovic, looking at the transcript she is referred to. If it can be broken down ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: All right. I will go back to line 8 on page 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Manning says, "Going to the 15th ..." And so I assume that all of the dialogue, without my reading it, for the following page, still has to do with the morning of the 15th. And I'm just jumping forward because the next question under the topic of the 15th, on page 14, Dean Manning says: "Did the Chief of Staff Obrenovic brief the commander Pandurevic on what happened in his absence?" And Mr. Simic says: "I wouldn't know about this, because I met Obrenovic on the ground floor and I briefed him quickly about the situation that I was having at the time." Now, that certainly conflicts with the story about having Mr. Jokic brief you on the 15th, when Mr. Simic, who was the duty officer who took over, claims that he briefed you on the 15th; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Simic did not brief me on anything. I didn't even see him. It was precisely the way I put it in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Simic is not telling the truth; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he's mistaken. Perhaps he didn't have the right time. Perhaps he mixed up the day or the hour. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to jump way forward in the line of questioning. What would reflect Mr. Simic being the duty officer on the 15th and what would reflect that Dragan Jokic was not there on the 15th would have been the duty -- change of duty shift book, which is missing out of our group of evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty shift book would not be the sole factor reflecting the situation. As I've already said, as to who was on duty and at what time, as I've already explained, is seen in the work book, the logbook, the regular combat report, and of course the duty shift book. Now, we have everything else except the duty shift book. So everything that you're saying now can be read out from any of the four documents enumerated. So of the five documents, we have four, and in them you can clearly see what happened and when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- In the duty work book it's clear that Nenad Simic became duty officer on the 15th, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll get to that as we come to those documents. I want to go back to Mr. Simic's statement on page 14, line 22. Dean Manning says: "I'm also interested in the whereabouts of Dragan Obrenovic in that period but to make it a small period, from the 11th to the 15th of July, detail for me where you know Obrenovic was." Nenad Simic replies: "I think during that time - I don't know. I know that Obrenovic came to the command during that period, engaged some people, met some people, solved some problems." And then I would like to skip on down to line 17. "Okay. Before you go, when Obrenovic tasked your referent Bojanovic after midnight on the 14th, where did he send, what did he give him to do?" And the last line of 22 -- I'm sorry. That's irrelevant. I don't know why it's underlined there. Anyway, Mr. Simic says that he's the one who briefed you on the morning of the 15th of the situation, as duty officer; isn't that right? I'm just asking you: Isn't that what Mr. Simic said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Simic said, but I explained to you exactly how it was. Specifically, this part of your question. As for the previous bits that you have read to me, it is true that Major Simic is generalising there. He knew that Obrenovic had been there on the 11th and that he came and went. But I defined this very clearly. I said I arrived on the 13th in the afternoon, that I almost spent the whole day at the command, I went to the engineering section, the detachment, that afternoon. I spoke about it in very precise terms. I think Simic is merely generalising. If you read it like that, it may appear this way or that way, or however you choose to interpret it, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not my interpretation, Mr. Obrenovic. It's how the Trial Chamber interprets the evidence that is placed before it. But I'd like to go now to what is marked as D18/3. And if we could provide the copies to the witness, please, that is, the OTP interview with Mico Gavric on 28 November 2001. Mr. Obrenovic, you already stated that you don't know who Mico Gavric is; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this statement, I know that he's an officer from the Bratunac Brigade command, but I can't remember whether I met him. I don't know the man. I've read the statement. That's all I can say about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to make that clear. You've read all of the statements provided in your case, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read very many statements. There were certain statements, such as those by the Bratunac Brigade, that I did not think were particularly relevant. I may have just skimmed through those. It was a truckload of paper. You can't possibly expect me to have detailed knowledge of every single statement that there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, I sympathise with you. I understand the truckload of paperwork that was received, believe me. In this statement by Mico Gavric, could we please turn to page 55, line 13. Dean Manning says: "When you went to Zvornik on the 14th, did you see any --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. This only has 46 pages, so I can't find page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the wrong Gavric, I believe. There's a couple of them. This is another one which we -- it would be best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that, you know, a different name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have on mine marked Mico Gavric. Is there another one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On mine is Milisav Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think they copied the wrong statements, because mine is 28 November 2001, of M-I-C-O G-A-V-R-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. It's different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the best way is put that relevant part on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And provide Mr. Obrenovic the correct copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Can you pull the relevant part? Because I need my copy to read from. Okay. Mine's the only copy. Your Honour, since mine's the only copy of the correct statement, may I approach the ELMO for reading out as everybody is looking at it? I only have the one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S copy? I mean, this is something that I think the witness should have a chance to take a look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will clear this up after the break, and I'll come back to this witness. So I'll just put it back in the chair with the statements that haven't been provided back here. So I'll just continue this, Ms. Usher, after the break, when we have the correct copies of the statement. Thank you. I'll go on to I hope what is the correct statement, which is marked for identification purposes as D17/3, the interview of Nada Stojanovic. Yes, Your Honour. Do you have a copy of it, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an interview with Nada Stojanovic, and the whole part of the interview, questioning by Mr. Bursik has to do with her being transported to Orahovac on the day of the 14th and what she saw and what happened. And I will go ahead and take you forward to page 34. I can't read the lines. I don't think there are lines on this one. It says the day -- Mr. Bursik says: "The day that you went to Orahovac before leaving the barracks at Zvornik, did you see the chief of staff, Obrenovic?" Ms. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but that's not what I have on page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he could have a moment. The pagination, of course, is different for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nada Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I think that this was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 39. Page 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for your assistance, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 39, Mr. Bursik says: "The day that you went to Orahovac before leaving the barracks at Zvornik, did you see the chief of staff, Obrenovic." Nada Stojanovic replies: "The only time I saw him was when I came back that night, when I came back to the barracks, I saw him in the compound, but we just passed each other. " And that was the 14th that Ms. Stojanovic is referring to. Are you aware that Ms. Stojanovic has stated that in her statement before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you don't think Ms. Stojanovic saw you in the compound on the evening of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. If we could have a reference to where Ms. Stojanovic actually says it's the 14th, that would be helpful, because it's not what this record says in front of me. I don't doubt counsel that she must say 14th somewhere, but that -- it's not said -- there's not in fact a proper foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sinatra, maybe you could show the -- show us the paragraph where she is indicating the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will have to find that at the break too. I cannot come up with it at this moment. And I really apologise for the lack of organisation, but I do have another witness that we could go on to at this time, and he is Milan Maric. He's now marked as -- is he D26? Did you add him?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: D20/3, Milan Maric. And could we be provided with copies of that, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. Do you have a copy, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a document, a statement by Milan Maric, taken on the 30th of June, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And starting on page 33, line 18, Milan Maric says: " -- Let's start with Mr. Manning's question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's 12.05 and I resume this conversation. Tell me what, in your account, and what in Obrenovic -- what in your account and what in Mr. Obrenovic's accounts differ. Milan --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't see that, line 18, "in view of literally," that's what my document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wish I -- after all these years I should speak B/C/S, Your Honour, but I'm delinquent in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's very understandable that you only have your assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Not long ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I've been here since 1996. You'd think I would have learned it since then. It's page 31 in the B/C/S version, line 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 31.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Manning asked: "Tell me what in your account and what in Mr. Obrenovic's account differed." Milan Maric said: "He was very, Obrenovic was very dissatisfied when I couldn't confirm especially about the 13th, in the afternoon. 13th in the afternoon and going on the 14th, that I couldn't tell him that he was with me and he was saying: 'Well, where else could I have been but with you?' And obviously he didn't like my story very much. Maybe the other people told him the story that pleased his ears more, and maybe they agreed to do certain things, and maybe he didn't like me or the way that I perform my duties or the way that we cooperate. I assume that was the reason that I was transferred." That's what Mr. Maric said, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You've just read it out, and as you were reading, you realised probably that every second word is "perhaps" or "he may have" or and everything is "perhaps" or "maybe" or "he may have." What is true, though, is that I sent Maric to Snagovo on the 13th and I stayed back at the command. Logically, I was not with him. Secondly, I said that I had a logbook that I showed Maric. I read clearly everything that was in there when I spoke to Maric. And once he had finished this, I showed him the logbook. So I had no reason to force Maric to do anything, nor was I in a position to do anything like that. He says it himself, maybe this, maybe that. He wrote it in his own hand. He wrote it out clearly, everything that was happening. He was the duty officer on the 12th and the 13th. And then the next duty officer also wrote everything down in the logbook. So I really don't know why he's putting forward so many assumptions here, so many different assumptions. Maybe he was unhappy that he had been transferred to Sokolac, so maybe he's taking his revenge here, but it's not for me to say really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you tried to talk -- you talked to Milan Maric before your interview with the OTP, didn't you, in April of 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This conversation took place following my conversation with the Prosecutor in 2002. Maybe a month or so later. I think Maric says it himself in this statement. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you tried to persuade Mr. Maric to confirm that you were present at Snagovo on the night of the 14th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't try to get him to provide an alibi for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to do anything like that. I had all the documents and all the documents that I've given the Office of the Prosecutor. Why would I have needed to convince him to do anything? It was all written there. You saw it yourself. I just found it in the papers, the fact that he was a duty officer on the 13th and that he was the commander of a company, whereas here he claims that he wasn't. I believe that he simply might have reminded me of a detail that I had lost track of. But these are his impressions, and they're not well founded, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you just stated that you showed Milan Maric the logbook, and you're talking about one of the logbooks that you kept hidden from the OTP and from the Defence during the period of 1999 through 2003; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the logbook of the operations duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade for that period of time. I refer to it as the blue book some days ago. The colour of the cover is blue, and that's what I showed Maric. I showed him only the page that he wrote himself in his own hand. I didn't keep any secrets, as you can clearly see, because you have the document yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you just gave the documents to us after you pled guilty on June 3rd, 2003, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My lawyers forwarded these documents to the Office of the Prosecutor following my plea, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was June 2003 before we saw these documents; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Milan Maric, after his conversation with you, was transferred out of the Zvornik Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The answer to your question is necessarily a complex one. The truth of the matter is that Milan Maric was not transferred after this conversation. As to when exactly he was transferred, this is clearly stated in the order for his transfer. His transfer was a result of a reorganisation of the Army of Republika Srpska, pursuant to the Dayton Accords and to a decision by the SFOR commander in the year of 2000, 1999. The Army of Republika Srpska had to be whittled down. We had about 200 people in Zvornik and this had to be down to 50. Major Maric was the war commander of a battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. There was a proposal for him to stay there at the command. However, the corps commander, General Zivanovic, or rather, my apologies, General Andric and the 5th Corps, he was transferred to the corps command at Sokolac. However, I must point out that the law on the Army of Republika Srpska and you can run a search yourself, the right to transfer someone with the rank of a general, or major, would have to be granted by the defence minister, and I was only the brigade commander. Despite this, my proposal was for him to stay with the Zvornik Brigade. And you must have these documents, because we did forward these documents to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the Tribunal. So those documents show clearly what Maric said, any way, maybe, or it is my impression that these are all speculations that hardly ever have anything to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to follow up on this: When Mr. Jokic wouldn't cooperate with you, he was transferred by General Andric to Sokolac too, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Jokic was transferred to the 5th Corps, but much earlier.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure. I know it was much earlier, but I don't know which year exactly. This may have been in 1998, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that transfer in just a moment. I want to finish with Mr. Maric. On page 34, line 4, Milan Maric, Dean Manning says: "Okay. Start on the 13th. When were you with Obrenovic?" Milan Maric says: "On the 13th, 6.00 in the evening, he ordered me, in my office, to go to the location of Snagovo, meaning that I saw him also on the 14th in the morning." "So, you saw him at 1800 when he ordered you to go to Snagovo. When was the next time you saw him?" "In the morning of the 14th, at about 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning." So from what Mr. Maric says it appears that you were gone from Snagovo from 6.00 in the evening on the 13th until 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning on the 14th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right, no. Again, for the umpteenth time, I went during the night between the 12th and the 13th, around midnight or just past midnight. I spent the rest of the night there, the morning of the 13th, and I stayed there until about noon, the 13th, and just past noon on the 13th I came back to the barracks, Zvornik. That's where I spent the afternoon, until about 9.00 in the evening I was in the barracks. Not only in the barracks, but also I went to the engineering department, the barracks, the duty officer, my office, and then back to Snagovo. I spent the night there at Snagovo, the night between the 13th and the 14th. Quite possible, yes, those were units, the second half of the night between the 13th and the 14th, I got involved in deploying the MUP forces from Doboj in their positions. I looked for Maric when I needed him. This line of ambush was maybe between two and three kilometres long, and I never said that I had spent that whole night with Maric. What could I have been doing with him? He was a company commander. So when I needed him, I sent for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when Maric says that he wasn't with you and he didn't see you at Snagovo from 1800 on the 13th to 8.00 or 9.00 on the 14th, then he's mistaken; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether we saw each other that night. He may as well be right. What I'm telling you is that we were involved in an activity. We were setting an ambush. And I was dealing with the MUP company for most of that time. So he may not have seen me at all. He may be right here, though. I never said that I spent that entire night with Maric, because I was involved in specific activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did say that you spent it at Snagovo, though, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, but please try to understand. Snagovo is an area that's a bit bigger than this courtroom, so not everyone could see everyone else there. It's about ten different hills, an area covering about ten kilometres. And we were setting up defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only logical that he may not have seen me at certain moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he said he didn't see you at all during the period from 1800 in the evening until the next morning, at Snagovo. And you do recognise that that's what Mr. Maric says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what he stated if I look at the statement. But I told you a moment ago that I went to Snagovo on the 13th. Probably it was at about 9.00 in the evening. So it's quite logical that he couldn't see me, because I had been in the barracks, in the office, up until then. And then as dusk was falling, I came there and we set up the units for the defence. We were expecting fighting to begin and we weren't standing next to each other. So that means he may not have seen me. I'm just explaining why he may not have been able to see me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You do remember in your debriefing on the 18th that you discussed five or six Muslim children were captured by the VRS on the front, don't you? Do you remember that, on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of July there were several, five to six, Muslim children that were captured on the front, in the Zvornik zone of responsibility. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that some children were brought. I don't know where from, the road to Parlog.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have stated in your statements before that Mr. Jokic assisted them to get through the minefield and back to their families, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the Muslims called and thanked you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't call me specifically. They just called the Serbs. That's what they said. But Jokic was the one who had taken them through the minefield between our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to the morning of the 15th. After you and Colonel Vasic were in your office trying to decide how to solve and save Zvornik, you discussed the possibility of letting the column pass through; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you called General Miletic for permission to let the column pass, and he said: No, you have to fight. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I tried to come into contact with my commander, and then the command of the Drina Corps, but there was nobody up there. And, yes, I spoke to General Miletic and he said exactly what you said, as you summarised it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the same General Miletic that gave you access to the documents that you seized in 1999 from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general is the same, but he did not give me access to the documents. I have already explained how I came by those documents. I said so two or three days ago in detail, and I can repeat it if you like. But Miletic didn't give me access to that. I think that he learnt about it when the documents appeared here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we'll go through this chain of custody a little bit later. I just wanted to make sure that this was the same General Miletic. He was located in -- was he located in Mali Zvornik in 1999 and 2000, at the warehouse facility there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the spring of 1999, he was there for four or five days, looking through the documents. And I visited him twice, following orders from the corps commander, the general of the 5th Corps, General Andric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to you letting the column pass through. And basically, when you opened the column up, because Zvornik could not stand against this column, you allowed their peaceful passage, more or less, with a little scattered firing here or there; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is too much generalisation, that that isn't actually how it was. I couldn't say that three days of heavy fighting and all the 200 -- 40 dead and 200 wounded, that can't be considered to be sporadic shooting and fighting on a small scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, basically, by your preserving the integrity of Zvornik, you were a hero by making that decision with the local people, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Misstatement of the evidence. I think it's been clearly established or stated previously who made that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the decision made by Colonel Vasic, or the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain, please. On the 15th, when we met in front of the headquarters here, Vasic asked around about the police captain, Captain Jankovic, who had been taken prisoner, and he asked me whether I had seen with my own eyes that there were so many men, that the forces were so strong, and he was surprised by that. So when I informed him of it, all his first proposal, yes, they should really be allowed to pass through, because the command of the 28th Division had a radio relay and they called from that captured person, Captain Jankovic, they asked for free passage. And Colonel Jankovic suggested that. Now, my position was such, my duty was such, and position was such, that it wasn't up to me to make that decision. So I said who we had called up to ask for approval and permission. But we did not receive permission, and in the meantime, the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic arrived, and both I and Vasic suggested that to him. I told him first in my office. I said that we had agreed and we felt that the column were to be let through. But his reaction was to prohibit that. He did not allow the column to be passed -- the column to pass through. And afterwards, so on the 15th, in the afternoon, the night between the 15th and 16th, and the 16th up until 2.00 p.m., we were engaged in serious fighting. It really was very heavy combat. Over 200 people were wounded, many people were killed, our own people, our own men. And I don't like having to mention these killed persons to illustrate a point, but that's how it was. So it was only after this that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic made the decision and in agreement with Semso Muminovic, the officer, commanding officer on the opposite side, was the corridor opened. And I said that it was my impression that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was facing great pressure, especially from the Main Staff, because they were opposed to this. That is how I saw it. So the decision as to whether to open the corridor or not was not a decision that I made. I really did not make that decision. Had I had the right to make the decision, I would have made it, and wouldn't have called anybody. I would have taken the decision on the 15th, in the morning, and there wouldn't have been all those dead people. I believe to the present day that that was a mistake, but I just didn't have the authority to make the decision on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we hope that we could revisit the document D17/3 and D18/3 after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention that for the moment we will have to withdraw the testimony regarding Nada Stojanovic, because in the OTP statement there's no reference to the day that she was in Orahovac. But I can coordinate it with Mr. Butler's statement, saying what day she was there, but I'll have to find that tonight and if you'll allow me just to reintroduce this tomorrow. We can't confirm the date unless we corroborate it with some other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think we have copies of Mico Gavric, but I see that my help is gone. So I'm going to go on to another document, which, for identification purposes, has been marked D6/3. And I don't know if I have anybody to help me with this at the moment. I can go back to another question real quickly regarding Milan Maric. I'd like to go back to his statement, which we had covered already. And I would like to ask Mr. Obrenovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that Milan Maric was one of the witnesses used by the OTP to confirm witness tampering in getting the denial of your provisional release; right? Should I break that down, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you like. But since there's no objections, you could go your way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that Milan Maric was interviewed by the OTP when you were requesting provisional release; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it that the OTP talked to Maric for their regular investigations, and it coincided by chance that they could use this to oppose my provisional release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you are aware that your provisional release was denied because of allegations by the OTP of witness tampering; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, it's calling for a conclusion on why the Trial Bench at that time did anything, which is completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he knows and he read the documents, I think he has a right to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. You should not answer this kind of question. You may put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you are aware that your request for provisional release was denied; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were explained that one of the reasons that provisional request was denied was the argument put forth by the Prosecutor that you were tampering with witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the reasons that was stipulated in the decision was the fear that I would influence witnesses. Nothing specific was stated, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now I'd like to go back to Mico Gavric. I think we've just -- did we just -- no. I'm sorry. This is a document prepared by Mr. Obrenovic. Can you tell me: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Obrenovic? And just for clarification, this is D6/3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes. I haven't got time to read through the entire document, but yes, I would say that that is what I once typed out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a document that was prepared by you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking. As I say, without entering into the details to see whether anything has been altered, but roughly speaking, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's a document that you prepared in anticipation for your interview with the OTP in April of 2000, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you provided the Prosecutor with a copy of this itinerary through your attorney during your interview with the Prosecution in 2000, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although my pages aren't numbered, I would like to go to the 13th of July, 1995 and ask you to review that day quickly. Now, Mr. Obrenovic, during July 13th, 1995, in this itinerary you've prepared for the Prosecution, you never mention any call from Drago Nikolic on the evening of the 13th telling you about the arrival of any prisoners, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could we go to the 15th of July, 1995, about maybe eight lines down. You start with: "Around 9.30." And might I remind you: This was prepared before your review of all OTP statements; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. At the time, I had none of these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Around 9.30, I arrived to the barracks in Zvornik via the old road. Colonel Vasic showed up immediately and we discussed the possibility of letting the Muslims through. I asked the Drina Corps command for permission. There was nobody there, while at the Main Staff, General Miletic did not allow that and hung up on me." And then it goes on to discuss your meeting with Colonel Vasic. And the truth is, there's no mention about any debriefing by Dragan Jokic on the morning of the 15th, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing is mentioned with respect to any incriminatory acts, not only for the 15th, but as you said a moment ago, for the 13th as well, and all the other days too. And you can read it for the 14th. No incriminatory acts were mentioned by me at the time. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, this document was given to Mr. Jokic by your joint counsel at the time, Krstan Simic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I thought not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know that Mr. Simic had given Mr. Jokic a copy of your itinerary, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know that Mr. Simic was trying to coordinate the stories between you and Mr. Jokic by giving Mr. Jokic a copy of your proposed itinerary; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that Mr. Simic didn't give me anything that was written by Jokic. This is the first I hear of it, of him giving Dragan Jokic these papers of mine. If I had wanted to give this to him, I would have given it to him myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: You just stated that Mr. Simic had never given you anything relating to Mr. Jokic's case; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember that right after Mr. Jokic's first interview with the OTP, that Mr. Simic had given you the original audio copies of that interview? I'm sorry. Not the original, but the Defence copy of the audiotapes of that interview.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so they're not still in your custody, then; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have what the Prosecution gave us, all those statements and tapes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about before your interview with the OTP in April 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this line of questioning as inappropriate, unless counsel will lay the foundation that they intend for Mr. Jokic to withdraw his attorney/client privilege with Mr. Simic and intend to have Mr. Simic take the stand to put some credibility to these suggestions, and/or Mr. Jokic to do the same thing. Otherwise it's speculating into areas of attorney relationships, and this kind of speculation and assumption of facts without anything to back it up is really inappropriate, and I don't see the relevance of it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can get a subpoena on Mr. Simic, I would love to have him come testify, but Mr. Simic has explained to lead counsel that he gave the audiotapes to Mr. Obrenovic. Because we've requested them. We never could get our copies of the audiotapes, and that's where we have been told they have been possessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on this issue is crucial to your case or not. And my suggestion is that you may ask a statement from this person and exhaust all the possible means at your hands to gain some evidence. If you failed, you may raise this issue again to the attention of the Chamber, and we'll see what we could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think there is a potential that I may be a witness in this area at some point because of -- I really don't want to talk about it in open session, but we will come to this when we're discussing the suppression of the statements and the conflict of interest with the attorneys at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could come to it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So may I ask him whether he has the audiotapes in his possession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, do you have the audiotapes from Mr. Jokic's interview in December 1999 your in your possession?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have in my possession tapes of the interview that I gave. I didn't even listen to them, because I also received a transcript, so I just read through that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, do you have in your possession the audiotapes from Mr. Jokic's interview with the OTP in April of 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. Simic had said that he had given them to you, he would be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although we are not acquiescing to the acceptance of the accuracy or reliability of the intercepts, I would like to ask him a question about one of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you agree with the way we suggested?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You mean present the evidence and let the Trial Chamber decide on the weight to give it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, no, no, no, no, no. We are using this document at the moment, and later on we'll discuss whether we should admit it into the evidence. The weight matter is something far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I think I'm going to skip the question. I'd like to preserve my running objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it does not affect your objections. Your running objections is still there. If you want to ask some questions concerning these intercepts, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I think I'm going to move on for today. I'll think about it overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obrenovic, you know that Mr. Nikolic has completed his testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you and Mr. Nikolic have been housed in the same location -- I'm sorry. Let me retract this. Mr. Nikolic said that written reports from Main Staff and Main Staff security would not necessarily go to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, communications between security didn't go through the command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please elaborate? I don't think I've understood your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'm going to put it in another way, in that normal rules of command and communications don't necessarily apply when there is a Main Staff presence during a special operation, do they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if Mladic is there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If Mladic is there or Beara is there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be possible for them to issue any order that they see fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go to Dusko Vukotic. We mentioned him earlier. Now, he was the assistant chief of staff of intelligence, starting in 1994, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He held the rank of captain first class?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 14th and 15th of July, you had him stationed at a special location high above Zvornik to receive communications, didn't you, and that's at Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kula Grad, yes. Not only to receive messages and communications, but rather to maintain contact with the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Plus could he visually see the approach of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably could, from Kula Grad, he could have seen them entering the villages of Bajrici, Samari and Liplje. In some places at least. This is a wooded area we're talking about so as they were passing clearings, yes, he would have been able to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarification for the Trial Chamber, Kula Grad is an ancient medieval fortress built high on a cliff overlooking Zvornik from about the thirteenth century, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kula Grad is a geographical term referring to a village which is there, including three hillocks in the area, the space between them, plus a medieval fortress, and the village itself. It's a geographical name for the village and the buildings there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The view from this fortress is a military location that has been maintained for centuries and centuries because of the view that you have up there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One section of the fort, the east battlement, more specifically, from there, you can see the river Drina and that section of the valley, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vukotic, do you know what kind of radio equipment he had up there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he had a Motorola piece of communications equipment, using ultra shortwave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your signalman that you had with you had a Motorola that could receive his radio signals, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My signalman had an RUP-12, which was not compatible with the other piece of equipment. So whenever we needed to get in touch with Vukotic, Vukotic would go to the artillery platoon, who were stationed there at Kula Grad and were using the same sort of communications equipment that I was using. So that's how we got in touch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The artillery division, when it communicated with your RUP-12, it didn't necessarily have to go through the switchboard, did it, at headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None of those messages with Mr. Vukotic were intercepted, were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been intercepts for the tactical conversations, as the Prosecution called them. Every day. He used the signal Vuk, or Wolf, and there have been many intercepts between myself and him and other units he was speaking to. Vuk was the code that he was using.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of the communications with Vuk, Captain Vukotic, were concerning combat operations or legitimate military operations on the night of the 14th and the 15th; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there and he took part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated on your direct that you didn't know anything about the CZ. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have misheard the interpretation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think CZ is a Serbian term for civilian protection organisation. You stated in your direct testimony that you didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the question perhaps refers to the reply I gave Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic on the 15th, when we spoke in the corridor. He asked me why the burials were not being carried out by the civilian protection, and I said I was not even aware of them having to do it. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to your direct testimony, where Mr. McCloskey was questioning about the burial of the Muslim soldiers on the 16th or 17th, and you said that it was a normal function of the engineering department. And he asked you about the CZ and you said you didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I never used the term "CZ," so perhaps if counsel has the transcript number, she can help us out. But that, it's just confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilian protection organisation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what civilian protection is, yes, in Zvornik, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said that you didn't know anything about that in your direct testimony, that was not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. If this is a form of impeachment, we would -- I think it's appropriate to have the source clear and at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra. If you want to challenge this witness's testimony, you had better point to us the specific page and line of this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will come back to that with the exact line in the transcript, Your Honour, but I'd like to go forward with my questioning about the civil protection organisation, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may use the term the civilian protection organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had jumped ahead. You were aware that Commander Pandurevic, or Pandurevic, when he returned on the 15th, he asked you why you hadn't engaged the civilian protection organisation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He asked why the burials were not being carried out by the civilian protection, not why I hadn't engaged them to do it. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By him asking you that question, wasn't he inferring that you should have taken care of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me what had been ordered, and I told him that I didn't even know that any such thing had been ordered. That's all we said about civilian protection. I don't know what he meant. I'm only telling you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilian protection organisation is the organisation responsible for burials and terrain restoration in the civilian section of Zvornik municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that's one of their duties, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the engineering company is not really authorised to participate in burials. That's the duty and responsibility of the logistics company, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the rules, it's the logistics units that should clear the terrain or do the sanitisation, the logistics battalion and one of their units, but it's also the right of any of the commanders, on account of the given circumstances, to order a specific activity. Under the rules, strictly speaking, it is not the duty of the military police to engage in direct combat, but, as we have seen, under the circumstances, we were forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like a direct answer from you from my question. The engineering company is not authorised to participate in burials; it is the responsibility of logistics, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference in the rules to anything being forbidden to anyone. If you mean the specific concept of sanitisation, or asanacija, then the rules specify that a logistics unit should be in charge of that. That's in the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the civilian protection organisation, if you know, since I don't know that you are familiar with this organisation, they're the ones responsible for contacting the Red Cross or the United Nations when there's any kind of emergency situation, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be the case, but I really can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since there was no authority for the engineering company, that was commanded by Dragan Jevtic to engage in this, then, on the other hand, the chief of engineering certainly did not have any authority to requisition this civilian service, did he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having said anything like that. Was your question in relation to a set of rules --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Engineering rules. Engineering rules. The chief of engineering could never have the authority to requisition a municipal organisation to undertake an engagement such as these burials, could he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the rules, no. The civilian protection --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About asanacija, or terrain restoration, this is not a term that is just specific to the rules of the JNA or to the rules of the VRS, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the rules applied in any other army, so I can't talk about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know that it might be a general provision in any military in the international community; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it may be so, but as I said, I haven't read any of the other rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And terrain restoration, as it's written in the JNA manuals, is really written in there to prevent epidemics and protect the public health, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. That's one of the purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to Mr. Nikolic's testimony, and I assume that you read the transcripts from his testimony, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't had an opportunity to read the transcript of his testimony. I have read the statement that he gave the Office of the Prosecutor prior to his testimony, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I won't refer to his testimony, but if Mr. Nikolic had said that the burial operation that took care of the problems at the Kravica Kravica warehouse strictly run by equipment from the Bratunac Brigade, that would make sense, because Kravica is in the Bratunac zone of responsibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. If they didn't have the equipment, the corps command could have taken steps to bring equipment from just about anywhere. Whoever was in charge of the burials, if they had no machines, they could have easily hauled them in from just about anywhere, on civilian or military authority, regardless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is a CZ in Bratunac also, isn't there? I'm sorry. Civilian protection organisation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't ask you about any of Mr. Nikolic's testimony. If you say that you are not familiar with it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I told you is that I read his statements, the statements that he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. But I never had a chance to read the transcript of his testimony, because it was never forwarded to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When supposedly you were notified that prisoners were being sent to the Zvornik area of responsibility, it's my understanding that you responded that: We can't accept that responsibility because the commander is not here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two parts to your question, and my answer has two parts also. When you say "supposedly," it wasn't supposedly; it was exactly as I said it was. As for the latter part of your question, I didn't say that we could not accept that because the commander was there, but rather that we couldn't accept it unbeknownst to our commander and without explicit approval from our commander, not merely because he was absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to just go back to your telephone or radio message from Drago Nikolic, informing you about this operation on the 13th. As we stated, that was not intercepted, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not radio message. This was no radio message and it was not a phone -- it was a phone conversation by phone line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the only evidence that we have that this conversation took place is to borrow from Mr. Karnavas, four ears and four eyes of you telling us that that's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Asking the witness to speculate on the state of the evidence. I would certainly disagree with that, that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the question has a point. Maybe the form of the question is not correct. And I think Ms. Sinatra just wants to ask whether there's somebody else besides Mr. Obrenovic when he was talking -- he was receiving the telephone call from Drago Nikolic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's exactly what I'm trying to get an answer about. And as far as I know, the only evidence we have that this conversation took place was -- is Mr. Obrenovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, we have no other evidence that Drago Nikolic informed you of this operation on the evening of the 13th, other than you saying so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence. Mr. Butler's report deals with the subject in depth. There's many inferences. The good part of the Prosecution's case was based on that there must have been communication at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us hear what Mr. Obrenovic is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber has said you can answer the question, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, I don't know if this particular conversation was ever intercepted. Among the evidence submitted to us by the Office of the Prosecutor, I have read no such thing. But yes, such a conversation did indeed take place, and not via radio link, but rather, by phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're not aware of any other evidence that supports this telephone conversation, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I've seen any, not that I've been shown any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've read all of the intercepts and all of the statements provided by the OTP, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for all, I don't know, but I've read a number of them, yes, quite a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the relevant statements. We'll stick with that. Thank you. Just to clarify matters: Your duty officer on the 13th, Sreten Milosevic, I believe, was the duty officer on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, Sreten Milosevic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He gave you the information that 3.000 prisoners were possibly coming in your direction from their capture on Konjevic Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not how it was, and I don't remember having said that. What I did state with respect to that matter was that when, on the 13th, a little after noon, I returned from Snagovo, that the duty officer, Captain Sreten Milosevic, informed me about having talked to the corps commander and that he had said that the road was blocked between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, and that the Muslim units had not managed to pass through further than that. And later, in the course of the day, I learnt from various other sources that the figure bandied about was 3.000, that there were 3.000 prisoners from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and Kasaba. But there was no talk of them coming to Zvornik, and I don't think I ever said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only thing I'm trying to get is that other than your allegation that Drago Nikolic informed you that these prisoners were to be killed, there is no other evidence other than a legitimate military operation of the transfer of prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right on that score. You mean looking at it today? Actually, I'm not quite sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the evening, nobody else knew of the intention to kill these prisoners. You might not have even known. The only evidence we have is a call, assumedly, from Drago Nikolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who knew about it, all the people who knew. I just said that Drago Nikolic called me up, and I told you what he told me. He mentioned the people that I've already mentioned myself during my testimony. And as I said, I believed him, quite simply. Now, who else knew about it, I really can't say. I read what Nikolic stated, but I don't know the details of it, no specifics. I believed him. I believed that all the people he mentioned as knowing about it did actually know about it. Perhaps I was wrong. It was -- I made my -- I drew this conclusion on the basis of what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he didn't mention any names but that someone would be getting in contact with the people in your area. Isn't that what you said? So you didn't mention any names when you were talking to Drago Nikolic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Misstatement of the evidence. This really messes up the record and is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, we could not understand your question at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll try to organise my thoughts a little better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You want to help?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: More instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not quite. I wouldn't put it in those terms, Your Honour. But the gentleman did indicate that he -- all the people that -- mentioned the people that -- that I've already mentioned myself. He didn't mention any people. He said, as I understood it, and as we discussed yesterday, that Drago Nikolic said that everybody knew it, including the commander. I think he never said that he mentioned particular people. So I just want to clarify that point. And maybe there's some confusion going on. But as far as I know, he never mentioned any particular names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. If Mr. Karnavas's evidence can be accepted, I agree with him 100 per cent. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's my precise objection to all of this. The lawyer is trying to put in evidence. It's just absolutely wrong, doesn't reflect the facts of the case, and the witness, I'm sure, can answer the question if he's given a specific question, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going from the sublime to the ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Karnavas just make a statement of how he understands the conversation. But he's not -- it may not reflect the facts. So we need some more questions put by Ms. Sinatra to this witness to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify Mr. McCloskey's side bar comment from the sublime to the ridiculous. I hope I'm the sublime and the other team is the ridiculous. There's a lot of side bars going on here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to save time, just put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were a conversation between you and Drago Nikolic, if there were evidence supporting this, your statement, when referring to the conversation, said -- never mentioned anybody else by name; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm following you correctly, and I apologise, but you did have at least four questions there, your question plus all the subquestions. First of all, you said if there was a conversation. My answer to that question was yes, there was a conversation. The second question, or subquestion, well, it's just slipped my mind. I apologise. What was the second thing you asked?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they're really prepositional phrases instead of questions. But if there were evidence supporting your statement with Drago Nikolic -- do you want to answer that one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't shown anything like that. I didn't see anything along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this alleged conversation, you never mentioned anybody else's name, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the telephone conversation between myself and Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned several names, or rather, Drago Nikolic mentioned the following names: Mladic, Beara, Popovic, and later on Jasikovac, when he asked for Jasikovac to be placed at his disposal. So in that entire conversation, those were the names we mentioned, the name of our commander, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And again, there was no intercept recording this conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read any, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, transportation of prisoners, based on your military expertise, transportation of prisoners from one zone to another zone is viewed as a legitimate military operation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's further verified if the caravan on the 14th is being led by a United Nations white APC; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it myself. It was only later on, after all these events, that I heard stories told about some of the UNPROFOR equipment that was used and the APCs that were mentioned, not just one, but several of them, that they had been captured and used, among other things, also for accompanying the convoy. But I did not know that at the time. I learnt that somewhat later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that the soldiers on the buses were wearing UN uniforms too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that story told later on. I didn't know at the time. And I don't know whether all of them wore them. I heard that some of them did, did have uniforms, UN uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarification: The duty officer's office in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters doesn't face the road, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
